title: Ezra Sets Out for Jerusalem
overview: Ezra, a priest and expert in the Law of Moses, travels from Babylon to Jerusalem with a Persian king's letter that pays for temple worship and gives him authority to set up justice there.

parts.label: Ezra's family line (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: Ezra's ancestry is traced back to Aaron, Israel's first high priest, showing he is a true priest. The list skips generations, so "son of" can mean descendant; the Seraiah named here is probably the high priest killed when Babylon took Jerusalem long before.

parts.label: A teacher with royal backing (vv. 6-7)
parts.note: Ezra was a scribe, meaning a trained expert in the Law of Moses and how it applied to life, not just a copyist. The writer credits the king's generosity to "the hand of the LORD," a phrase that keeps returning in these chapters.

parts.label: The four-month journey (vv. 8-10)
parts.note: The group left Babylon at the start of the Jewish new year and arrived four months later, a slow pace for a large company traveling with families and belongings. Verse 10 sums up Ezra's purpose in three steps: study God's law, live by it, then teach it.

parts.label: The king's letter and gifts (vv. 11-20)
parts.note: This official letter is written in Aramaic, the government language of the Persian Empire, and uses "king of kings," a standard Persian royal title. It lets any Israelite who wishes go with Ezra and sends silver and gold from the king, his seven advisers and the Jewish community to pay for temple sacrifices.

parts.label: Supplies and tax freedom (vv. 21-24)
parts.note: Regional treasurers west of the Euphrates must give Ezra silver, wheat, wine and oil up to set limits, and temple workers are freed from taxes. The king's reason is frank: he wants to avoid the anger of Israel's God, which fits the Persian habit of honoring the gods of the peoples they ruled.

parts.label: Authority to judge, and praise (vv. 25-28)
parts.note: Ezra may appoint judges for the Jewish communities of the region and enforce both God's law and the king's, with penalties as harsh as death, exile, seizure of property or prison. The text then shifts into Ezra's own voice as he thanks God for the king's favor and gathers leaders to go with him.

think: Ezra is described as learning something, living it, and only then teaching it; how much does it matter to you whether the people who teach or lead you actually practice what they say?
